items.title: RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent

official_metadata.title: Title: RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent
official_metadata.history: Submission history From: Huan Zhang [ view email ] [v1] Thu, 15 Oct 2026 12:45:08 UTC (1,888 KB) [v2] Mon, 2 Nov 2026 09:12:51 UTC (1,818 KB)
official_metadata.abstract: Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. However, adapting self-improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge. We propose \textbf{RSIFlow}, a \textbf{R}ecursive \textbf{S}elf-\textbf{I}mprovement framework that integrates adaptive work\textbf{flow} orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution. RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component-specific improvement workflows. The meta-agent then distills workflow outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration. Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution. Code is available at this https URL .

The Meta-Agent converts task experience into parameter updates. It constructs training data 𝒟 t \mathcal{D}_{t} from execution trajectories and environmental feedback, then optimizes the following objective starting from θ t \theta_{t} : min θ ⁡ ℒ ⁡ ( θ , 𝒟 t ) = 𝔼 z ∼ 𝒟 t ​ [ ℓ ⁡ ( θ , z ) ] . \min_{\theta}\;\mathcal{L}(\theta;\mathcal{D}_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\bigl[\ell(\theta;z)\bigr]. (4) Here, z z is a training sample or sample group, and ℓ \ell is the method-specific loss. Our default update uses SFT to learn from successful trajectories collected during task execution. Reusing these trajectories reduces the exploration cost of acquiring training data. The candidate inherits the updated parameters θ ′ \theta^{\prime} alongside the parent’s Harness and Artifacts. We also evaluate an RL-based model-update variant, with details provided in App. B.3 .

The Meta-Agent uses execution feedback to select a component set ℐ t ⊆ 𝒞 \mathcal{I}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{C} , where 𝒞 = { Action , Skill , Planning } \mathcal{C}=\{\mathrm{Action},\mathrm{Skill},\mathrm{Planning}\} . It follows a localize–refine–generate–validate procedure to produce new implementations H ^ t ℐ t \widehat{H}_{t}^{\mathcal{I}_{t}} . The candidate Harness replaces the selected components while preserving the others: H ′ = H t Task [ ℐ t ← H ^ t ℐ t ] . H^{\prime}=H_{t}^{\mathrm{Task}}\left[\mathcal{I}_{t}\leftarrow\widehat{H}_{t}^{\mathcal{I}_{t}}\right]. (5) The replacement operator rewrites the selected components and preserves the rest. Revisions may change prompts, context organization, memory retrieval, planning and reasoning rules, tool orchestration, or internal verification, subject to the corresponding interface and permission constraints. For example, jointly revising memory retrieval conditions and planning rules constitutes a single Harness update. Model parameters remain fixed.

We separate five rounds of training-stage evolution from evaluation on the fixed 744-task reporting set. For each evaluated evolution horizon n n , we first complete n n evolution rounds on training batches and then evaluate the resulting frozen system. When the Artifacts route is selected, the Task-Agent revises task-specific outputs using execution feedback, and the resulting outcomes provide evidence for Meta-Skill evolution. Revised training artifacts remain local to their original tasks and are not transferred to unseen tasks. During reporting, the selected Artifacts refinement procedure can be applied to each evaluation task through one additional feedback-guided revision. The fixed-Artifacts ablation follows the same five-round training protocol, with reporting-time refinement performed only after training.

items.title: The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents

official_metadata.title: Title: The Trinity: Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents
official_metadata.history: Submission history From: Weidong Tang [ view email ] [v1] Mon, 26 Oct 2026 18:03:34 UTC (42,027 KB) [v2] Fri, 30 Oct 2026 04:15:41 UTC (42,027 KB)
official_metadata.abstract: Abstract: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.

evidence.quote: Modules are pure functions of supplied public records, without hidden-state access or environment actions. Only Memory may declare explicit carry ; hypothesis refutation requires observed contradiction. All protocols may emit typed readiness signals, while Loop resolves execution. Orchestration assesses applicability, relevance, and trust within a fixed host-exposed tool set. Evolution updates module configurations with θ \theta fixed.

Capabilities and protocols have a many-to-many relationship: the tree groups shared requirements, while protocols locate module updates. Hypothesis consistency can involve Memory organizing evidence, Inference checking compatibility, and Planning ranking informative tests; the same Memory module can support several requirements. Explorer retains node modules; Creator uses the same tree structure and consolidates its next Base Harness. Evaluation-time skills are prepared separately (Section 4.1 ); they are not stored, evolved, inherited, or routed in the tree.

For Explorer, capability-driven RSI builds a Harness tree aligned with the capability tree. At each node, Explorer executes admitted worlds with inherited and local modules. Evolver compares successful and failed trajectories using public observations, actions, and host-assigned outcomes to identify node-specific improvements. It develops reusable modules through host-registered bindings in the six-protocol library (Section 2.2 ), refining interfaces, bounded configurations, or implementations. Updates record node, predecessor-version, episode, and executable-example references. Before local updates, the host validates evidence, ownership, interfaces, lineage, and typed input–output assertions; ancestor modules remain preserved. Bindings use public context and permitted memory under a fixed runtime policy. Multiple bindings per protocol may coexist, with model calls determining execution order. Admission verifies grounding and executability; evaluation measures performance. Creator evolves only upon verifier-detected failures. At each iteration’s end, validated proposals are consolidated with existing Base Harness modules, merging complementary modules and removing near-duplicates. Section 3.5 details persistence, selective inheritance, and consolidation.

Explorer plays every benchmark with the frozen backbone (Appendix D ), and each instance uses the best-scoring compatible node Harness under the Oracle setting. Every node Harness starts from H 0 , which has no learned module, and combines the inherited modules at their retained versions with the node’s local modules; a benchmark at c → \to d → \to a therefore uses the modules of c, c → \to d, and c → \to d → \to a, subject to selective inheritance (Figure 12 ). At each node, Explorer plays the admitted training levels with these modules, and Evolver compares successful and failed trajectories to create or revise local modules; the host validates evidence, ownership, interfaces, and version lineage before every update, and ancestor modules are preserved. An updated parent is inherited only if it achieves strictly more host-verified task completions than the previously inherited modules under the same validation tasks, trial count, and budget; otherwise the previous modules are kept. A local module overrides an inherited module bound to the same identifier. Module calls take public inputs and return structured advice without advancing the environment, with at most two calls per step and none forced.

items.title: TTHE: Test-Time Harness Evolution

official_metadata.title: Title: TTHE: Test-Time Harness Evolution
official_metadata.history: Submission history From: Jun Nie [ view email ] [v1] Thu, 9 Jul 2026 05:53:39 UTC (229 KB) [v2] Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:30:33 UTC (218 KB) [v3] Wed, 4 Nov 2026 09:02:27 UTC (218 KB)
official_metadata.abstract: Abstract: The behavior of an LLM agent is determined not only by the underlying model, but also by its harness: the executable program that constructs context, invokes tools, verifies intermediate results, and recovers from failures. Existing approaches typically optimize harnesses on training or development data and freeze the resulting programs at test time, limiting adaptation to shifts in task distributions, failure modes, and tool interactions. We ask whether the harness can instead be optimized during evaluation using unlabeled execution traces. We introduce Test-Time Harness Evolution (TTHE), which treats the executable harness as the state of test-time adaptation. On each unlabeled test batch, TTHE iteratively evolves a population of candidate harnesses through agentic proposers that reason over execution traces and explore diverse edit directions. A judge selects a candidate using execution traces and execution-derived proxy signals. The selected harness determines the current batch's outputs and initializes adaptation on the next. Crucially, the solver, proposers, and judge operate through different harnesses around the same frozen LLM, without weight updates, access to final-answer labels, or a separately trained adaptation model. Across six execution-grounded benchmarks spanning text-to-SQL, competitive programming, software engineering, data-science coding, terminal-based tasks, and agentic tool use, TTHE improves fixed ReAct-style baseline harnesses through persistent, inspectable program adaptation. These results recast test-time adaptation for LLM agents as evolution over executable control programs and identify execution-derived proxy reliability as a central challenge for robust unsupervised agent improvement.

evidence.quote: We evaluate TTHE on six execution-grounded benchmarks, where it improves fixed ReAct-style baselines and yields inspectable grounding, verification, and recovery policies. On the evaluated BIRD dataset, TTHE achieves 48.7 % 48.7\% mean execution accuracy over three runs, compared with 12.7 % 12.7\% for the fixed baseline. A separate ten-run execution-result consistency-voting control achieves 16.0 % 16.0\% . Harnesses selected by DeepSeek for each BIRD batch also improve MiMo V2.5 and GPT-5.5 over their respective fixed-harness baselines on the corresponding batches, without further harness evolution. These results provide evidence of cross-model transfer of the evolved task-solving procedures. Search diagnostics reveal non-monotonic effects of search budget and distinguish candidate-availability limitations from selection errors. Together, these findings support executable harness adaptation as a practical path to test-time self-evolution in LLM agents.

BIRD shows the largest gain, from 12.7 % 12.7\% to 48.7 % 48.7\% mean execution accuracy. Gains also occur on LiveCodeBench, SWE-bench Verified, and DS-1000, and extend to terminal-based tasks and multi-service tool use: Terminal-Bench 2.1 rises from 55.1 % 55.1\% to 67.8 % 67.8\% , and claw-eval from 48.9 % 48.9\% to 69.4 % 69.4\% . Across these settings, the same frozen backbone supports task execution, program revision, and candidate selection. The complete procedure thus obtains useful test-time harness updates without modifying model weights or introducing a separate repair model.

Executing DeepSeek’s selected harness on the corresponding BIRD batch, without further evolution, improves MiMo V2.5 from 32.0 % 32.0\% to 56.0 % 56.0\% and GPT-5.5 from 36.0 % 36.0\% to 68.0 % 68.0\% (Table 5 ). Backbone variation tests whether other models can use the evolution procedure; this experiment instead tests whether they can use its resulting programs. The gains show that a batch-specific harness can benefit execution models other than the one that evolved it.

items.title: Hyperagents

official_metadata.title: Title: Hyperagents
official_metadata.history: Submission history From: Jenny Zhuoting Zhang [ view email ] [v1] Thu, 19 Mar 2026 20:50:08 UTC (6,553 KB) [v2] Sun, 1 Nov 2026 21:28:39 UTC (6,555 KB)
official_metadata.abstract: Abstract: Self-improving AI systems aim to reduce reliance on human engineering by learning to improve their own learning and problem-solving processes. Existing approaches to self-improvement rely on fixed, handcrafted meta-level mechanisms, fundamentally limiting how fast such systems can improve. The Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM) demonstrates open-ended self-improvement in coding by repeatedly generating and evaluating self-modified variants. Because both evaluation and self-modification are coding tasks, gains in coding ability can translate into gains in self-improvement ability. However, this alignment does not generally hold beyond coding domains. We introduce \textbf{hyperagents}, self-referential agents that integrate a task agent (which solves the target task) and a meta agent (which modifies itself and the task agent) into a single editable program. Crucially, the meta-level modification procedure is itself editable, enabling metacognitive self-modification, improving not only the task-solving behavior, but also the mechanism that generates future improvements. We instantiate this framework by extending DGM to create DGM-Hyperagents (DGM-H), eliminating the assumption of domain-specific alignment between task performance and self-modification skill to potentially support self-accelerating progress on any computable task. Across diverse domains, the DGM-H improves performance over time and outperforms baselines without self-improvement or open-ended exploration, as well as prior self-improving systems. Furthermore, the DGM-H improves the process by which it generates new agents (e.g., persistent memory, performance tracking), and these meta-level improvements transfer across domains and accumulate across runs. DGM-Hyperagents offer a glimpse of open-ended AI systems that do not merely search for better solutions, but continually improve their search for how to improve.

evidence.quote: The DGM-H can achieve self-improvement in coding comparable to prior self-improving algorithms.

The DGM-H significantly outperforms the original DGM in both domains (p < 0.05), reflecting the limitations of the original DGM’s fixed instruction-generation mechanism when applied to non-coding tasks (Figure 2).
The DGM-H achieves higher median performance than DGM-custom on the test tasks in both domains, although the difference is not statistically significant (p > 0.05) (Figure 2).
Hence, the transferred meta agent (i.e., the procedure that generates task-agent modifications) carries most of the transferable self-improvement capability.

They demonstrate useful task-level and meta-level improvements and their transfer across domains; they do not yet establish unbounded or self-accelerating improvement, which we view as the long-term motivation that DGM-H contributes to (Section 7).

items.title: Harness Updating Is Not Harness Benefit: Disentangling Evolution Capabilities in Self-Evolving LLM Agents

official_metadata.title: Title: Harness Updating Is Not Harness Benefit: Disentangling Evolution Capabilities in Self-Evolving LLM Agents
official_metadata.history: Submission history From: Minhua Lin [ view email ] [v1] Thu, 28 May 2026 22:16:14 UTC (1,619 KB) [v2] Wed, 4 Nov 2026 20:26:58 UTC (1,629 KB)
official_metadata.abstract: Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly deployed as systems built around editable external harnesses, including prompts, skills, memories and tools, that shape task execution without changing model parameters. Harness self-evolution adapts such agents by updating these harnesses from execution evidence. Yet it remains unclear whether a model's base capability in task-solving predicts its capabilities in harness self-evolution: which models produce useful harness updates, and which actually benefit from them? We analyze two harness self-evolution capabilities: (i) harness-updating, the capability to produce useful persistent harness updates from execution evidence; (ii) harness-benefit, the capability to benefit from updated harnesses during task solving. Our analysis reveals two findings. First, harness-updating is flat in base capability: models from different capability tiers produce harness updates that lead to surprisingly similar gains; even Qwen3.5-9B's updates yield gains comparable to those of Claude Opus~4.6. Second, harness-benefit is non-monotonic in base capability: weak-tier models benefit little from updated harnesses, mid-tier models benefit most, and strong-tier models benefit less than mid-tier. We trace low gains at the weak tier to two failure modes: weak-tier models may fail to activate relevant harness artifacts, or activate them but fail to follow them faithfully. These findings suggest investing capability budget in the task-solving agent rather than the evolver, and targeting harness invocation and long-horizon instruction following in agent training. Our source code is publicly available at this https URL .

evidence.quote: First, harness-updating is flat in base capability . When we fix the task-solving agent and vary the evolver model, models from different capability tiers produce harness updates that lead to surprisingly similar gains, and no evolver dominates across all substrates. Our case studies further show that even the Qwen3.5-9B evolver produces harness updates whose downstream gains match those of Claude Opus 4.6, despite a large gap in base capability.

Second, harness-benefit is non-monotonic across base-capability tiers . Mid-tier models (e.g., GPT-OSS-120B) benefit most from updated harness, and strong-tier models (e.g., Claude Opus 4.6) reach the performance ceiling and benefit less. The weak-tier end, however, is not explained by the same ceiling argument: with the largest headroom above their base capability, models like Qwen3-32B might be expected to benefit most, yet they benefit the least. Our in-depth analysis identifies two failure modes that explain this weak-tier gap: (i) harness activation failure : weak models often fail to invoke relevant harness artifacts (e.g., skills) during task-solving; and (ii) harness adherence failure : even when the harness is loaded, weak models fail to adhere to it due to weak instruction-following over long-horizon tasks.

Agent Harness. We use agent harness to denote the external, non-parametric context and infrastructure through which an LLM is deployed for task execution Yao et al. (2022) ; Ning et al. (2026) ; Lee et al. (2026) . Formally, at evolution step t t , the LLM agent is defined as: A t = ( f , H t ) , A_{t}=(f,H_{t}), (1) where f f is the agent’s model backbone and H t H_{t} is the harness state after step t t . Following common harness self-evolution settings Zhou et al. (2026) ; Lin et al. (2026c) , we keep f f fixed and only update editable components of H t H_{t} (e.g., prompts, skills, memories), and fix other components such as tool interfaces and execution policies.

items.title: EvalResearchBench: Can AI Agents Build Their Own Feedback for Recursive Self-Improvement?
items.reason_zh: v1/v2 的297个正文/表格/图注节点完全一致；标题由 Design Their Own Evaluations 改为 Build Their Own Feedback for Recursive Self-Improvement。旧 move 到通用评测仍可复用，不计入Harness方法；当前canonical题名已是新版但version仍为1，需后续真实版本绑定。

evidence.quote: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) relies on evaluation feedback to assess progress and guide further research, yet repeatedly running complex benchmarks is costly and slows iteration. Human experts reduce this cost by selecting benchmark subsets or designing compact suites. We ask whether AI agents can automate this design process and introduce EvalResearchBench (ERB), a benchmark for autonomous evaluation research. evidence.quote: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) in scientific research aims to improve agents’ research capabilities through their own experimental experience. Scientific agent swarms can pursue this goal when one agent’s findings and implementations advance another’s research. Two obstacles stand in the way. A failed experiment does not reveal whether its hypothesis or its implementation was at fault, and a program without overall gains can hide components that other agents need. We introduce SwarmRSI , a framework in which a swarm improves its research by evolving the research states its agents inherit, including hypotheses, programs and experimental evidence. Feedback-Guided Swarm Mutation uses other agents’ feedback to decide whether to revise a hypothesis or its program. Complementary Swarm Recombination tests retained hypotheses on other agents’ programs and combines complementary components. Recursive Swarm Evolution returns every outcome to a shared graph that guides which state each agent updates next. SwarmRSI achieves state-of-the-art performance across three benchmarks, scoring 76.2 on OpenProblems, attaining a 44.4% Match-SOTA rate on NatureBench, and earning medals on 81.8% of MLE-Bench Lite tasks. Across 90 NatureBench tasks, 77% of the best programs descend from feedback-guided mutation or recombination. Biologists further validate two generated programs in studies of intestinal and splenic immunity. The code is available 1 1 1 https://github.com/EvoScientist/SwarmRSI .

items.title: OSWAM: An Effective World Action Model with One-Step Action Generation

official_receipt.title: Title: OSWAM: An Effective World Action Model with One-Step Action Generation
official_receipt.abstract: Direct-policy World Action Models (WAM) have demonstrated the benefits of decoupling action generation from explicit future visual prediction for efficient inference in autonomous driving and embodied control. However, they still require tens of denoising steps to achieve competitive action quality, incurring substantial latency and hindering real-time deployment. Simply reducing the number of denoising steps will collapse the nonlinear multi-step denoising trajectory into coarse updates, substantially degrading action quality. To reduce the denoising steps while enabling real-time action generation, we present an effective world action model with one-step action generation, namely OSWAM, for autonomous driving and embodied control. We argue that it is the absence of structured action priors in random noise initialization that forces direct-policy WAMs to recover coherent action sequences through iterative denoising. Hence, we construct imagination tokens to initialize the diffusion process, providing physical priors and action-conditioned representations. We further introduce privileged information distillation with future conditioning to enhance future-aware action generation. As a result, OSWAM can efficiently and effectively generate high quality actions in just one diffusion step. Our experiments demonstrate that OSWAM achieves comparable or even better results in both autonomous driving and embodied control than direct-policy WAM and Joint-WAM that require tens of steps. It obtains approximately $3\times$ speedup over direct-policy WAM baselines and supports real-time compiled inference with latency as low as 40ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. items.title: No Channels Left Behind: Understanding Diffusion Acceleration through Residual Gates

official_receipt.title: Title: No Channels Left Behind: Understanding Diffusion Acceleration through Residual Gates
official_receipt.abstract: Training acceleration methods for diffusion transformers, such as REPA and dispersive regularization, are commonly explained by additional supervision, spatial-structure priors, or improved feature geometry. We revisit this view and uncover a striking internal change: the AdaLN-Zero residual gate $\alpha$, which directly controls how conditioned updates enter the residual stream, is substantially reorganized by these methods. This observation motivates our hypothesis that acceleration arises, at least in part, from reshaping the residual gating pathway rather than solely from the feature structures explicitly imposed by auxiliary objectives. Supporting this view, accelerated models are markedly more sensitive to perturbations of $\alpha$, and their gate geometry reflects semantic relationships among classes. We further introduce the normalized participation ratio (nPR) to characterize the channel-wise organization of the gates and find that, across REPA teachers, projector architectures, and radial-objective targets, broader gate participation accompanies better generation quality. Guided by this insight, we propose a simple teacher-free radial objective that promotes broader gate participation through feature-norm regularization, without pairwise feature comparisons. On ImageNet $256\times256$ with SiT-B/2, our method improves FID over dispersive loss while increasing mean gate participation over timesteps and classes, further supporting the link between gate organization and training acceleration. Our results identify residual-gate reorganization as a measurable axis of diffusion training acceleration and suggest a simple direction for further acceleration.

items.title: TernScope: Model-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient Ternary Endoscopic Segmentation

official_receipt.title: Title: TernScope: Model-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient Ternary Endoscopic Segmentation
official_receipt.abstract: Edge medical segmentation must reconcile small model size, high accuracy, and fast inference. TernScope addresses this tradeoff through model--hardware co-design, learning a compact segmentation network whose low-bit operators also simplify hardware execution. Split-channel large-kernel blocks preserve spatial context with limited computation, while branch fusion removes redundant inference paths. Ternary Progressive Quantization-aware Training (TPQ) then adapts the fused network from deep to shallow layers, through the decoder, and finally to the input and prediction layers. All 25 convolutions use ternary weights and 8-bit activations, enabling packed storage and multiplier-free computation. The resulting model uses 0.2483 M parameters and 0.0949 GMACs while retaining competitive segmentation accuracy on in-domain and external datasets. Under the same 45 nm technology, TernScope reduces compute-array area by 88.46% compared with the original Gemmini, a systolic-array accelerator with 8-bit $\times$ 8-bit multipliers. These results demonstrate a path from accurate lightweight medical segmentation to compact low-bit hardware.
